title: Opinion: The cost of Ontario’s nuclear plan spirals. When will the province get serious?
html:
Ontario Power Generation is now reporting that the Darlington New Nuclear Reactor on which construction has barely begun, is already behind schedule and now projected to come in over its original $7.7-billion budget.Sammy Kogan/The Globe and Mail

Mark Winfield is a professor in the faculty of Environmental and Urban Change at York University. He is co-chair of the Sustainable Energy Initiative, and co-editor of Sustainable Energy Transitions in Canada (UBC Press 2023).

There are growing concerns over the costs of Ontario’s expensive and questionable nuclear strategy. With only one of the new-build projects under way – the small (300MW) reactor at Darlington – the province is already spending between $7-billion and $8-billion a year subsidizing the electricity rates that help pay for them. In effect, the province is hiding the actual costs of its plans from consumers.

This cost amounts to nearly half of the provincial deficit, and exceeds annual capital expenditures in areas such as education and health care by wide margins. The current arrangements likely represent the fiscal limits of this strategy. Last month the government began to modify its subsidy arrangements to reduce costs to the provincial treasury, particularly by reducing support to high electricity consumers.

Into this mix has come further bad news. Ontario Power Generation is now reporting that the Darlington New Nuclear Reactor, on which construction has barely begun, is already behind schedule and now projected to come in at more than its original $7.7-billion budget.

Although consistent with the track record of previous nuclear projects, this cannot bode well for the likely costs of the much larger Wesleyville and Bruce C projects. And, as a first-of-its-kind small reactor, whose construction was authorized by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission on the basis of an incomplete design, there remains the risk that even when completed, the new Darlington reactor may not work as planned, or at all. That is what happened with the last new-build reactor project in Canada, the MAPLE isotope reactors, in 2008.

Moreover, the refurbishment of the existing Darlington facility, which was announced in February 2026 as being completed “on time and on budget” has been followed by a series of shutdowns and requirements for additional work. The implications for the refurbishment of the much older Pickering B station – whose estimated costs at more than $26-billion would already be double those of the Darlington refurbishment – cannot give any comfort to Ontario electricity ratepayers or taxpayers.

In the meantime, the province’s reliance on fossil fuel-fired generation has been accelerating. Fossil gas-fired generation – and by implication the associated emissions of greenhouse gases and smog precursors – has quintupled, to at least 20 per cent of supply, since 2017, and is expected to continue to increase through the 2030s. The province has also announced that it has contracted fossil fuel-fired electricity (likely made using oil) from the United States over the winter of 2026-27. The growth in emissions from the Ontario electricity system has been so significant that it’s emerging as a key factor in driving the overall increase now being observed in Canada’s national emissions trajectory. That overall growth is being principally attributed to the electricity sector.

Beyond the dramatic growth in emissions, the costs associated with the province’s nuclear ambitions seem likely to undermine competitiveness, affordability and electrification itself, as electricity prices are driven upward. Worse, Ontario’s model is having national effects, as the same nuclear- and gas-centric focus seems to underlie much of the federal government’s Powering Canada Strong electricity strategy.

Ontario does have options for its electricity system other than a massive and enormously risky nuclear construction program – it just refuses to consider them. Ontario has been the subject of more efforts to develop and model alternative pathways for its electricity system, and the broader decarbonization of its energy system, than any other province in Canada.

Those options emphasize energy efficiency and productivity, renewable energy, energy storage and microgrids, options offering the potential to avoid the need for new-build nuclear projects and the high-risk, high-cost Pickering B and additional fossil-fired generation. But there is no public and independent regulatory process to assess whether the directions set by the provincial government represent the best options for the province in economic, environmental and energy security terms relative to the alternative pathways that have been identified.

That situation needs to change rapidly. The province needs to engage in a serious, objective assessment of its options for meeting future energy needs in the context of high levels of uncertainty. It needs to adopt a strategy to control energy costs, decarbonize the province’s electricity system, ensure energy security, and advance economic and environmental sustainability before it’s too late.
summary: Ontario does have options for its electricity system other than a massive and enormously risky nuclear construction program – it just refuses to consider them
